claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in the simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The simple solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi alloy has favorable plasticity and machinability.
The simple solid-solution structure of CoCrFeNiTi has only minimal lattice distortion.
Atomic-size mismatch in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is limited.
Limited atomic-size mismatch produces weak solid-solution strengthening in CoCrFeNiTi.
Weak solid-solution strengthening lowers barriers to dislocation motion.
Easier dislocation motion accounts for the alloy's plasticity and machinability.
Easier dislocation motion limits the hardness and yield strength of the as-cast alloy.
A controlled aging treatment can induce nanoscale secondary phases or short-range ordering in CoCrFeNiTi.
Aging-induced precipitates or ordering will increase lattice distortion.
Nanoscale precipitates or ordered regions will act as dislocation-pinning sites.
The additional lattice distortion and dislocation impediments produced by aging will increase hardness.
The additional lattice distortion and dislocation impediments produced by aging will increase compressive strength or yield strength.
The aged alloy will exhibit less plastic strain before failure than the as-cast alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies under quasi-static loading from room temperature through 600 °C.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes a single-phase structure, but the initial-state field permits a 'mixed structure,' which may mean a multiphase FCC+BCC state and is therefore inconsistent with a single-phase premise.
The intervention and mediator explicitly introduce secondary phases or ordering, whereas the boundary says the hypothesis is limited to behavior in the simple solid-solution state.
